_doc: consumed by server/routes/recommend.js. strategies[] mirror the AWS DR whitepaper's four strategies (RTO/RPO framing from https://docs.aws.amazon.com/whitepapers/latest/disaster-recovery-workloads-on-aws/disaster-recovery-options-in-the-cloud.html). tooling[] ids match workspace.tooling[] values in SPEC.md. regionSwitchBlocks[] are the official ARC Region switch execution block types as of late 2026 (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/r53recovery/latest/dg/working-with-rs-execution-blocks.html); 'layer' is the restore layer (L0-L7) where the block typically belongs, or 'any' for cross-cutting blocks; appliesToKinds uses component.kind values, empty when no seed kind maps to the block. replicationMechanisms[] carry rpoSeconds as the typical/unplanned figure (null = not applicable, architecture-dependent, OR not published by the vendor at all — read 'provenance' before rendering it). AUDIT K-9: every replicationMechanisms[] entry now carries 'provenance' and 'source'. provenance is one of: 'aws-doc' (the number comes from the cited AWS documentation page), 'vendor-claim' (the number is a commercial vendor's own published claim and nobody outside that vendor can check it), 'none-published' (the mechanism is real and AWS-documented but AWS publishes NO lag/RPO figure for it — rpoSeconds is null and any number you use must come from your own drill). Consumers MUST NOT render a vendor-claim or a none-published entry in the same visual shape as an aws-doc entry; that equivalence was the defect. 'source' is the page the entry was verified against, so a reader can re-check it without trusting this file.

strategies.name: Backup & restore
strategies.description: Nothing runs in the recovery region. Data is backed up (and copied cross-region/cross-account); infrastructure is redeployed from IaC after the event. Cheapest strategy, longest recovery, and the RTO is fictional until restore has been drilled end to end.

strategies.name: Pilot light
strategies.description: Data replication runs live and core infrastructure is provisioned in the recovery region, but compute is switched off. Cannot serve traffic without action: recovery means scaling up compute and switching traffic. The sweet spot for most tier-0/1 workloads that cannot afford always-on duplicates.

strategies.name: Warm standby
strategies.description: A scaled-down but fully functional copy runs continuously and can serve reduced traffic immediately; recovery scales it to full capacity. The official distinction from pilot light: warm standby can handle requests right now. Watch quota/capacity assumptions for the scale-up moment.

strategies.name: Multi-site active/active
strategies.description: Full capacity serves live traffic in multiple regions; there is no failover, only evacuation of a region. Requires application-level write strategies (write-global, write-local, write-partitioned) and makes every deploy multi-region forever. An architecture, not a DR add-on.

tooling.name: AWS ARC Region switch
tooling.summary: Managed multi-Region failover orchestrator (GA Aug 2025): plans of workflows/steps/execution blocks, graceful vs ungraceful modes, CloudWatch-alarm triggers, automatic plan evaluation every 30 minutes, PDF execution reports, data-plane execution from the region being activated. $70/plan/month.
bestFor: AWS-native stacks whose failover maps onto the official execution blocks (Aurora, EKS/ECS/ASG scaling, Route 53, ARC routing controls)
Making rehearsal routine: graceful-mode executions as scheduled recovery tests with built-in RTO measurement
Multi-application orchestration via parent/child plans
Removing the failed region from the recovery path (per-region data plane)
notFor: Provisioning infrastructure that does not exist yet (it scales/switches what is deployed; pilot-light provisioning stays with IaC/Arpio)
Data replication itself — the bytes must already be flowing
Non-AWS and third-party dependencies (partner allowlists, SaaS)
DynamoDB or Global Accelerator switchover (no such blocks; use custom Lambda actions)

tooling.name: ARC routing controls + Route 53 failover
tooling.summary: Route 53 failover records driven by ARC routing controls — on/off switches on a five-region quorum cluster with a 100% uptime SLA and safety rules (assertion/gating). Flipping a control flips a health check flips DNS, with zero control-plane calls during the event. $2.50/hr per cluster.
bestFor: Deliberate human-initiated regional traffic cutover (L7) on the data plane
Avoiding Route 53 control-plane (us-east-1) dependencies during an event
Guardrails on failover actions via assertion and gating safety rules
Pairing with Region switch plans (ARC routing control execution block)
notFor: Readiness checks (feature closed to new customers; use Phase 0 checks and Region switch plan evaluation instead)
Automatic health-probe failover if you want human decision-making (use plain endpoint health checks for that, with false-positive risk)
Anything below the DNS/edge layer

tooling.name: Arpio
tooling.summary: Commercial DR SaaS: discovers the environment as a resource graph, replicates both infrastructure config and data cross-region/cross-account on an RPO-driven recovery-point schedule (~15 min snapshots; seconds with real-time replication), launches a recovery environment in minutes, isolated network-sandbox drills, one-click failback, air-gapped bunker-account option.
bestFor: Managed-service-heavy stacks (Aurora, SQS, EKS, Secrets Manager...) that server-replication tools cannot cover
Teams with incomplete IaC coverage — the resource graph captures undocumented shape
Cross-account recovery: account compromise and ransomware scenarios, not just regional loss
Frequent low-friction drills via the isolated sandbox
notFor: Replacing runbooks, L6 verification, or the testing program
Traffic switching (pair with Route 53/ARC)
Third-party dependencies (allowlists, partner endpoints)
Resource types outside its supported-services list — verify per kind

tooling.name: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (DRS)
tooling.summary: Agent-based continuous block-level replication of servers into EC2 via a low-cost staging area; non-disruptive drills, point-in-time recovery, failback. ~$0.028/source server/hour. Successor to CloudEndure (discontinued 2024).
bestFor: On-prem / other-cloud servers recovering into AWS
Lift-and-shift estates with apps and databases on EC2
Legacy servers with no IaC — clones shape and bytes together
Ransomware recovery to a pre-encryption point in time
notFor: Cloud-native stacks with no meaningful EC2 fleet (EKS managed nodes, Aurora, SQS, Lambda, S3 give it nothing to replicate) — do not buy it for these
Managed databases (use Aurora Global Database / native replication instead; AWS scopes DRS to EC2-hosted, explicitly not RDS)
Rebuilding the surrounding environment (VPCs, DNS, IAM, queues, secrets)

tooling.name: GitOps / Infrastructure as Code
tooling.summary: Git as the source of truth for all infrastructure and app config; CI/CD and orchestration hosted outside the blast radius; the recovery region differs from primary by one variable; no console changes during an event; daily drift detection as a Phase 0 gate.
bestFor: Solving the 'rebuild the shape' problem reproducibly (L1-L4)
Symmetry: failover as a one-variable change, linted and continuously applied
Making every recovery test exercise the same path as every deploy
Static stability: fewer control-plane calls in the worst hour
notFor: Moving data — IaC replicates zero bytes
Resources changed by hand in the console (invisible drift until it is a gap)
Being the control plane inside the region it must recover

tooling.name: AWS Resilience Hub
tooling.summary: Declares RTO/RPO as policy and continuously assesses applications against it (including the Region-incident disruption type): resiliency scores, config/alarm/SOP/FIS recommendations, drift detection. ~$15/app/month; next-generation experience GA May 2026.
bestFor: Machine-generated RTO/RPO gap reports as decision-gate ammunition
Drift detection between quarterly reviews (SNS into the Phase 0 channel)
Auditing the inventory against what is actually deployed
A paved on-ramp to FIS fault-injection experiments
notFor: Orchestrating recovery (no failover button)
Performing replication (recommends only)
Substituting estimates for measured RTA/RPA — its numbers are configuration-derived hypotheses
Anything AWS cannot see: third parties, runbook quality, human readiness

tooling.name: AWS Backup (cross-region/cross-account copies)
tooling.summary: Scheduled or on-demand copies of recovery points (EBS, RDS, DynamoDB, EFS...) to another region and/or account; copies re-encrypted with the destination vault key. The floor under every other mechanism and the whole of the backup & restore strategy.
bestFor: Baseline protection for every stateful resource regardless of strategy
Cross-account copies against account compromise and insider threat
Tier-2/3 workloads on backup & restore
Point-in-time recovery from corruption/ransomware where replication would faithfully replicate the damage
notFor: Meeting minutes-level RPO (backup cadence is the RPO)
Fast RTO on large datasets (restore time grows with data size and is unknown until drilled)
Cold-storage recovery points (cannot be copied cross-region)

regionSwitchBlocks.name: ARC Region switch plan execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Embeds child plans for multi-application orchestration. AWS documents the DEPTH ('The hierarchy is limited to two levels, but one parent plan can include multiple child plans') but publishes NO number for the width — the block page says only that it 'limits the number of parent child plans'. CORRECTION (verified 2026-09-17): this entry previously said 'up to 25 children'. That is not an AWS quota. The Region switch quota table (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/r53recovery/latest/dg/quotas.region-switch.html) lists plans per account 10, execution blocks per plan 100, parallel execution blocks per step 20, CloudWatch alarms per trigger condition 10, and Route 53 health-check execution blocks per plan 25 — the 25 was that last row, misattributed. The binding constraint in practice is 10 plans per account, so a parent has at most 9 children before a quota increase. Child plans must support the same Regions and the same recovery approach (active/active vs active/passive) as the parent. Ungraceful mode starts children with their ungraceful configurations.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon EC2 Auto Scaling group execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Scales EC2 compute in an ASG; covers EKS self-managed/managed node groups backed by ASGs. Ungraceful mode takes a minimum-capacity percentage. Capacity is not guaranteed — AWS recommends on-demand capacity reservations for critical apps.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon EKS resource scaling execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Scales Amazon EKS cluster pods (deployment/replica scaling) in the activating region — the pilot-light 'turn the compute on' step for EKS workloads.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon ECS service scaling execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Scales ECS service tasks. No ECS kinds in the seed inventory; applies when ECS components exist.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: ARC routing control execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Flips ARC routing control states to redirect traffic to the target region — the final, data-plane traffic cutover. Place after a Manual approval block, which itself comes after the L6 verification. NOTE: 'cdn' was removed from appliesToKinds. A routing control flips Route 53 records; it does not reconfigure a CDN/WAF. CDN and WAF edge config — including the partner IP allowlist — is L5 'verify, don't create' work that must be complete BEFORE this block runs; if it genuinely must be automated, it is a Custom action Lambda, not a traffic block.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon Aurora Global Database execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Runs the Aurora global database recovery workflow: graceful mode performs a switchover (RPO 0); ungraceful mode performs a failover with potential data loss (RPO = replication lag at failure).

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Aurora Provisioned Scaling execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Scales Aurora provisioned cluster instances in the activating region to match the source region's instance class — right-sizes a thin pilot-light secondary before promotion.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Aurora Serverless Scaling execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Scales Aurora Serverless (v2) cluster capacity (ACUs) in the activating region.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon DocumentDB Global Cluster execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: DocumentDB global cluster recovery (added Dec 2025). Ungraceful mode fails over with potential data loss. No DocumentDB kinds in the seed inventory.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon Neptune Global Cluster execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Neptune global database recovery. Ungraceful mode fails over with potential data loss. No Neptune kinds in the seed inventory.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon RDS Promote Read Replica execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Promotes an RDS cross-region read replica to a standalone instance (non-Aurora RDS engines; added Feb 2026).

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon RDS Create Cross-Region Replica execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Creates a new cross-region read replica — a post-recovery workflow block that re-arms replication after a successful switch (requires both regions healthy).

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon RDS Switchover Read Replica execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Switches over an RDS for Oracle read replica to become primary; ungraceful mode promotes directly with potential data loss.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Manual approval execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Human gate: execution pauses until approved or canceled. Place before irreversible steps — data promotion in ungraceful mode, and always before the L7 traffic cutover. This is how 'human decides, machine executes' is encoded in a plan.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Custom action Lambda execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Runs a Lambda function for anything without a native block: ElastiCache Global Datastore promotion, secrets reconciliation checks, queue redrive kick-off, partner notifications, warm-up traffic, an edge/WAF configuration change that genuinely must be automated, and — importantly — the L6 functional verification, since no native block proves a business transaction. Ungraceful mode SKIPS this block type (and the Lambda event-source-mapping block), so never put a must-run data action here without checking that behavior, and never rely on it alone for a gate you need in an unplanned failover — pair it with a Manual approval block.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Amazon Route 53 health check execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Specifies the regions that application traffic is redirected to during failover — drives Route 53 DNS failover records via health-check state (data plane), no record edits during the event. LAYER CORRECTION: this was labelled L5 and is now L7. It moves LIVE PUBLIC TRAFFIC, exactly like the ARC routing control block, so it is the L7 cutover — and because the plan generator orders blocks by layer, an L5 label put the traffic flip BEFORE the L6 functional verification, which is the one ordering the product forbids (04-restore-layer-cake.md: 'shifting live traffic onto a stack that has never completed a business transaction converts a regional outage into a customer-facing incident you caused'). Place after a Manual approval block, which itself goes after L6 verification. NOTE: 'api-gateway' and 'cdn' were removed from appliesToKinds — API Gateway is the edge ENTRY POINT and a CDN/WAF is edge configuration; neither is a traffic switch. Both are L5 'verify, don't create' preconditions of this block (certificate valid in the recovery region, target groups/VPC links healthy, partner and WAF allowlists carrying the recovery egress IPs). Calling them traffic blocks told operators the plan would move traffic when it would not.

regionSwitchBlocks.name: Lambda event source mapping execution block
regionSwitchBlocks.notes: Enables/disables Lambda event source mappings — turn consumers on in the recovery region (and off in the impaired one) for SQS/Kinesis-triggered functions. Ungraceful mode skips the step.

replicationMechanisms.name: Aurora Global Database
replicationMechanisms.notes: Storage-level async replication to UP TO 10 secondary Regions (verbatim: 'An Aurora global database has a primary DB cluster in one Region, and up to 10 secondary DB clusters in different Regions'; the limit rose from 5 in May 2025 — do NOT 'correct' this back to 5, it has been wrongly flagged twice). Lag typically <1s; planned switchover is RPO 0, unplanned failover loses the lag. Aurora PostgreSQL can enforce an RPO ceiling via rds.global_db_rpo (min 20s). On an UNPLANNED failover AWS attempts best-effort write fencing (emitting an RDS Event on success and a different one on timeout) and attempts a point-of-failure snapshot of the old storage volume named rds:unplanned-global-failover-{cluster}-{timestamp} — see 07-tooling-region-switch.md; neither is guaranteed, and the snapshot is a system snapshot subject to the old cluster's retention period.

replicationMechanisms.name: DynamoDB global tables
replicationMechanisms.notes: MREC (default): multi-active, 'typically within a second', no replication SLA — watch ReplicationLatency; last-writer-wins conflict resolution. MRSC gives RPO 0 but AUDIT K-11 (verified 2026-09-17) — two constraints decide whether you can have it at all, and both were missing here: (1) 'A MRSC global table must be deployed in exactly three Regions' — three replicas, or two replicas plus a DynamoDB-managed witness Region you cannot read or write; (2) it can only be created from 'an existing DynamoDB table that contains no data' — 'Converting a single-Region table to a MRSC global table with existing items is not supported.' DO NOT draft an MRSC migration for a live table; it is not an available operation. Also: fixed Region sets (US/EU/AP, no crossing), no TTL, no LSIs, no transactions, no ReplicationLatency metric, and the consistency mode cannot be changed after creation.

replicationMechanisms.name: S3 Cross-Region Replication + Replication Time Control
replicationMechanisms.notes: CORRECTION (audit KB-4, verified 2026-09-17): this entry previously read '99.99% of objects within 15 minutes' and cited the RTC user guide, which does not say that. The user guide says 'S3 RTC replicates most objects that you upload to Amazon S3 in seconds, and 99.9 percent of those objects within 15 minutes'. The SLA is a SEPARATE document (https://aws.amazon.com/s3/sla-rtc/) committing to a Monthly 15-minute Replication Percentage, with credits below 99.9% (10%), below 98.0% (25%) and below 95.0% (100%). 99.99% is the DESIGN figure from the 2019 launch announcement. Quote the SLA number to auditors and name the SLA. Only replicates objects written after enabling — backfill with S3 Batch Replication.

replicationMechanisms.name: ElastiCache Global Datastore
replicationMechanisms.notes: Cross-region async replication for Valkey/Redis (node-based clusters), typically <1s lag, promote-to-fail-over, no SLA. This (or ElastiCache's own snapshot + cross-Region backup copy) is the mechanism for caches — AWS Backup does not cover ElastiCache or MemoryDB. Alternative, and usually the right answer: treat cache as rebuildable, and measure the cold-cache load the recovered database absorbs at cutover rather than quoting an RPO.

replicationMechanisms.name: ECR cross-region replication
replicationMechanisms.notes: Registry replication rules (cross-region/cross-account); 'The majority of images replicate in less than 30 minutes'; only content pushed or restored after configuration is replicated. UPDATED (audit KB-5, verified 2026-09-17): 'Repository policies, including IAM policies, and lifecycle policies aren't replicated' — but 'Repository settings aren't replicated by default, you can replicate the repository settings using repository creation templates. These settings include tag mutability, encryption, repository permissions, and lifecycle policies.' So the recovery-region registry does not have to be a bare image store; use a repository creation template. Images pullable in-region is an L2 gate.

replicationMechanisms.name: Secrets Manager replica secrets
replicationMechanisms.notes: Replicates secret value + metadata; same name (ARN differs only by region) so name-based resolution fails over; per-region KMS key per replica; rotation propagates automatically; replica promotable to standalone. AUDIT K-9: rpoSeconds was 60, which is an engineering estimate, not an AWS figure — AWS documents that rotation propagates but publishes no propagation-time number. Set to null rather than keep a made-up number in the same shape as AWS-documented ones. A secret store is judged on PRESENCE (does the replica exist, can the workload's own identity decrypt it) rather than on minutes of lag — see 13-secrets-pitfalls.md.

replicationMechanisms.name: KMS multi-Region keys
replicationMechanisms.notes: Same key material and key ID in each region — ciphertext decrypts on the other side without re-encryption. Existing single-region keys cannot be converted; key policies/aliases are per-region shape.

replicationMechanisms.name: AWS Backup cross-region/cross-account copy
replicationMechanisms.notes: SELF-CONTRADICTION FIXED (verified 2026-09-17 against 05-strategy-matrix.md rule 5, 'let the data layer veto'): 'pilot-light' was listed in strategyFit while rpoSeconds is 86400 (daily) and the pilot-light strategy in this same file declares an rpoRange of 'minutes'. A store whose only mechanism is a daily copy caps the whole workspace at backup-restore RPO no matter how warm the compute is — that is the article's rule verbatim — so pilot-light has been removed. If your schedule is genuinely tighter than the strategy's RPO, record the real cadence on the component and say so; do not re-add the row. RPO equals backup cadence (default daily; tighter schedules possible). Cross-account copies protect against account compromise. Copies re-encrypted with destination vault key; not available from cold storage. CORRECTION (verified 2026-09-16 against https://docs.aws.amazon.com/aws-backup/latest/devguide/working-with-supported-services.html): 'elasticache-redis' was removed from kinds — AWS Backup does NOT support Amazon ElastiCache (nor Amazon MemoryDB); neither appears on the supported-resources list. Route Redis/Valkey to 'elasticache-global-datastore', to ElastiCache's own snapshot + cross-Region backup copy, or to the rebuildable-cache path in 16-replication-mechanisms.md. Always check a resource type against the supported list before recording aws-backup-copy as its mechanism.

replicationMechanisms.name: AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery (block-level)
replicationMechanisms.notes: Continuous block-level replication of server disks into a low-cost staging area; sub-second to seconds RPO, minutes RTO for the servers it protects. EC2/on-prem servers only — AWS scopes DRS explicitly to EC2-hosted workloads, NOT RDS/Aurora and not managed services.

replicationMechanisms.name: Amazon MSK Replicator (Kafka)
replicationMechanisms.notes: AUDIT K-8: added. 'automatic asynchronous replication of data and consumer group offsets between MSK clusters', plus topic configurations and ACLs. Cross-Region and same-Region. CONSTRAINT: 'Both the source and target clusters must be in the same AWS account when replicating between MSK clusters.' Region-limited — check the supported-Regions list before planning on it. AWS publishes NO lag or RPO figure, so rpoSeconds is null: the number recorded on a Kafka component must come from observed lag in a drill. Note this is the ONLY managed cross-Region path for a streaming workload in this catalog — SQS and Kinesis still have none (see redrive-rebuild).

replicationMechanisms.name: OpenSearch Service cross-cluster replication
replicationMechanisms.notes: AUDIT K-8: added. Active-passive: a follower index pulls from a leader index, cross-Region or cross-account. Prerequisites that block adoption late: Elasticsearch 7.10 / OpenSearch 1.1+, fine-grained access control AND node-to-node encryption enabled, and index.soft_deletes.enabled on the leader (indexes upgraded from 6.x must be reindexed first). Max 20 connected domains; no UltraWarm/cold indexes; not on M3/T2/T3. 'You can't resume replication after it's been paused for more than 12 hours' — you must stop, delete the follower index and restart, which is an RTO event in itself. No published RPO: derive lag from the leader/follower checkpoint values.

replicationMechanisms.name: Amazon EFS replication
replicationMechanisms.notes: AUDIT K-8: added. 'After the initial replication is finished, Amazon EFS maintains a Recovery Point Objective (RPO) of 15 minutes for most file systems' — with a documented exception: 'if the source file system has files that change very frequently and has either more than 100 million files or files that are larger than 100 GB, replication may take longer than 15 minutes.' Not point-in-time consistent: changes transfer against a Last synced time, so the TimeSinceLastSync CloudWatch metric IS your RPA — alarm on it (Phase 0). Cross-Region and cross-account; supports fail over to the replica and fail back.

replicationMechanisms.name: Amazon FSx replication (type-dependent)
replicationMechanisms.notes: AUDIT K-8: added. rpoSeconds is null because the cadence is a schedule you choose, not a service property. FSx for NetApp ONTAP: NetApp SnapMirror, in-Region or cross-Region, 'Replication can be scheduled as frequently as every 5 minutes'; volume-level SnapMirror only, and 'Synchronous SnapMirror, including StrictSync, is not supported'. FSx for OpenZFS: on-demand snapshot replication 'between file systems within and across AWS Regions and accounts' via CopySnapshotAndUpdateVolume (full or incremental; cross-account via AWS RAM) — periodic replication is a scheduler you run over that API, not a managed cadence (https://docs.aws.amazon.com/fsx/latest/OpenZFSGuide/on-demand-replication.html). FSx for Windows and Lustre: no native cross-Region replication was verified for this edition — the cross-Region path is aws-backup-copy; check your exact type on the AWS Backup supported-resources list before recording it.

replicationMechanisms.name: EBS snapshot / AMI cross-Region copy
replicationMechanisms.notes: AUDIT K-8: added. rpoSeconds is null because the RPO is your snapshot schedule (Data Lifecycle Manager or AWS Backup), not a service property — record the actual cadence on the component. AWS names disaster recovery as a use case. Two drill surprises worth planning for: 'If you copy a snapshot to a new Region, a full (non-incremental) copy is created' — the first cross-Region copy is always full — and later copies are incremental only while the previous copy still exists in the destination and all copies share the same KMS key. Encrypted snapshots need kms:Decrypt/ReEncrypt/CreateGrant on both sides, the classic 'replicated ciphertext you cannot decrypt'. Limit of 20 concurrent copy requests per destination.

replicationMechanisms.name: Amazon DocumentDB global clusters
replicationMechanisms.notes: AUDIT K-8: added — it already had an ARC Region switch execution block in this file while being absent from the mechanism menu. 'A global cluster consists of one primary Region and up to 10 read-only secondary Regions… Latency is typically under a second.' AWS states 'a typical Recovery Time Objective (RTO) of under a minute' to promote a secondary, and 'The Recovery Point Objective (RPO) is typically measured in seconds, but this depends on the lag across the network at the time of the failure.' Not on v3.6; not on db.t3/t4g/r4; switchover and global failover are unsupported across mismatched engine versions (manual failover still works). Only the primary takes writes.

replicationMechanisms.name: Amazon Neptune global database
replicationMechanisms.notes: AUDIT K-8: added — it already had an ARC Region switch execution block in this file while being absent from the mechanism menu. 'A Neptune global database consists of a primary DB cluster in one region, and up to five secondary DB clusters in different regions' — FIVE, not Aurora's ten; do not carry the Aurora number across. Replication is at the storage layer, 'with latency typically under a second'. Two failover paths and they are NOT equivalent: managed planned failover relocates the primary with no data loss, while an unplanned outage needs the manual detach-and-promote, which turns a secondary into a standalone cluster and leaves the global topology to be rebuilt afterwards. Region-limited; no auto-scaling on secondary clusters; writes only on the primary.

replicationMechanisms.name: Arpio recovery points (snapshot-based)
replicationMechanisms.notes: AUDIT K-9: provenance is VENDOR-CLAIM, not an AWS-documented figure. The ~15-minute snapshot RPO is Arpio's own published claim (Standard tier, 'RPO >= ~15 min'); nobody outside the vendor can verify it and no AWS page states it. Do not render it in the same shape as an aws-doc row, and set replication.rpoMinutes on the component from what you OBSERVED in a drill, not from this number — 06-tooling-arpio.md says the same thing in prose. RPO-driven environment capture (infrastructure + data), cross-region and cross-account. SCOPE WARNING: 'supports SQS' means Arpio recreates the queue's SHAPE. No product moves in-flight SQS/Kinesis messages across Regions (16-replication-mechanisms.md, 'the hole in the menu'), so do not read this row's 15 minutes as an RPO for queue contents.

replicationMechanisms.name: Arpio real-time replication
replicationMechanisms.notes: AUDIT K-9: provenance is VENDOR-CLAIM. 'Real-time RPO' is Arpio's Premium-tier marketing language; the 5 seconds here is this catalog's reading of 'seconds', not a figure any vendor or AWS page states as a number. It is the least verifiable number in this file — treat it as a sales claim until a drill of yours produces an RPA. Rides native AWS replication (EC2, Aurora, DynamoDB, S3) under Arpio orchestration; Premium tier feature.

replicationMechanisms.name: Rebuild/redrive (no cross-region replication)
replicationMechanisms.notes: SQS and Kinesis have no native cross-region replication — re-checked 2026-09-16 and 2026-09-17; no such feature exists in either service. rpoSeconds is null because there is nothing to measure, not because it is fast. Queue/stream definitions are shape (IaC); in-flight data is handled by idempotent producers re-driving from a durable source, SNS cross-region fan-out, custom replicators, or a documented accepted-loss window. The decision must be recorded per component. NOTE what AWS does NOT document: the behaviour of in-flight messages during a regional impairment. 16-replication-mechanisms.md treats that as engineering inference and labels it as such — do not let any surface restate it as an AWS commitment. Kafka is the exception in this catalog: MSK has a managed cross-Region path (see msk-replicator).
